PLANT GUIDE · CORAL CACTUS

Coral Cactus

Euphorbia lactea ‘Cristata’ — variegated crested form

Not a cactus at all — a crested euphorbia whose growing point has stretched into a rippling fan of cream, sage, and blush pink, like coral lifted out of a reef. The fan cannot feed itself well, so it is grafted onto a sturdy green stock — two plants living as one, exactly as yours does in its planter.

🔍 Anatomy — Not a Cactus at All

THE CREST — one growing
point fanned into a line
THE GRAFT — fan riding
a plain green stock
THE SAP — cut it and
it bleeds white latex

A normal E. lactea grows as a spiny, candelabra-branched succulent shrub in dry tropical Asia. This one carries a mutation called fasciation: the growing tip flattens into a ribbon, and the stem fans out into folds instead of rising as a column. The pale tissue is variegation — low in chlorophyll, so it grows slowly and burns easily. Three proofs it is no cactus: it has no areoles (the little felt pads cactus spines grow from), its spines are small and paired along the ridges, and a cut bleeds milky latex — cactus sap runs clear.

🌿 The name: lactea is Latin for “milky” — the sap. Euphorbia honors Euphorbus, physician to King Juba II. Haworth described the species in 1812; the crested form exists only because growers keep grafting it, generation after generation.

🎛️ Conditions — Measured

Think bright shade at the edge of dry Asian scrub — strong light, almost no water standing anywhere. Harsh afternoon sun scorches the pale crest; too little light and the fan pales and stretches. The stock does the root work, but the whole plant still rots if it sits wet.

📋 The Care Card

LightBright indirect light, 4–6 hours a day — an east or west window is ideal. A south window works if the fan sits a little back from the glass; variegated tissue scorches in hard midday sun.
WaterSoak and dry: water deeply until it drains, then wait until the mix is completely dry before watering again. Roughly every 2–3 weeks indoors, less in winter. Overwatering is its main killer — when in doubt, wait.
SoilGritty, fast-draining cactus or succulent mix. The pot must have drainage holes, and never let it stand in a saucer of water.
FeedingA light balanced or cactus feed once a month in spring and summer. Nothing in winter.
TemperatureHappy at 60–85°F. Bring it in well before nights reach 50°F — it is not frost-tolerant, and cold plus wet is a fatal pairing.
RepottingEvery 2–3 years, in spring, one pot size up — wearing gloves (see the caution below).

✂️ Propagation — Kept Alive by Grafting

  1. Honest first: the crest cannot be grown from seed, and a fan cutting rooted on its own grows very slowly and weakly. Your plant’s form is kept the way it was made — by grafting, usually onto a plain Euphorbia neriifolia stock.
  2. In spring, wearing gloves, cut a healthy section of crest. Rinse the milky sap off the cut faces and let them dry.
  3. Cut the top flat on a rooted stock plant, set the crest piece squarely on it, and bind the join firmly with tape or an elastic band.
  4. Keep warm in bright indirect light until the union knits — a few weeks — then remove the binding.
  5. Forever after: rub or cut off any plain green shoots the stock pushes out. Left alone, the vigorous stock outgrows and starves the fan.

🩺 Troubleshooting

Pale, stretching fanToo little light — move it brighter, still indirect.
Bleached or brown patchesSunburn — pull it back from hard direct sun.
Soft, dark, mushy baseRot from overwatering — stop watering; if it spreads, cut back to clean tissue and re-graft.
White cottony tufts in the foldsMealybugs — its main pest, with scale — dab off with rubbing alcohol on a swab.
Green arms sprouting lowThe stock asserting itself — prune them off so the fan keeps the food.
🐈

Keep it up high, away from animals. The milky latex sap irritates skin and eyes and is toxic to cats and dogs if chewed. Wear gloves when you cut or repot it. ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435.

🪸 Two Plants in One — Reading Your Photos

Your fan shares a long green planter with other crested companions, over a pale gravel mulch that suits it well — it keeps the crown dry and shows off the colors. Grow it as the sculpture it is: bright shade, a dry pot, and a shelf of its own above cat reach.
